paragraphs: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Saturday it has set up a task force "to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials". Task Force Iron Gate is based in Tampa, Florida. CENTCOM said it will coordinate with other US agencies on stopping weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams from crossing Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Al Jazeera described the move as an expansion of a months-long naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz. CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said the task force will reinforce the blockade's success at sea. CENTCOM also said a US aircraft disabled the St. Kitts-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman. It said enforcement since July has redirected 147 vessels that complied and disabled five that refused.

Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defense secretary, told Al Jazeera that if President Donald Trump orders an escalation, it would likely hit economic and infrastructure targets, unlike Operation Epic Fury, which he said focused mainly on military ones. That is his assessment, not an announced plan.

Iran's IRNA agency reported explosions on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. Trump confirmed new strikes on Qeshm a day earlier, calling them "minor", and said Tehran still wants a deal as Qatari-mediated talks continue. Iran's IRGC Navy said two oil tankers struck sea mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's formal response to the task force was not reported in the source text.

Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 33 people, including women and children, were killed in Saudi air strikes on Saturday, according to the BBC. The Houthi-run Saba news agency said 39 others were injured. The claim has not been independently verified, and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has not commented.

Footage on Al Masirah, a Houthi-run television station, showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town east of the capital, Sanaa. The bodies of young children could be seen, and injured people were carried to hospital on stretchers.

The BBC said the war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited because of the Iran war. A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane landing. The Houthis then targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia and Saudi ships in the Red Sea. Major fighting has since resumed between the Houthis and forces backing the Saudi-supported government.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province reportedly killed 30 people. The Houthis blamed the Saudis, while government forces said the Houthis fired a missile at the site. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
Hours before the al-Shariyah strike, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading toward Riyadh. Houthi leader Mahdi al-Mashat has vowed revenge for the latest attacks.

UFC chief executive Dana White said on Saturday he is flying to Washington to meet President Donald Trump on Monday, after Trump publicly asked him to become White House press secretary. Trump posted on Truth Social: "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" The BBC said it was unclear whether the offer was genuine.

Speaking at a news conference after a boxing event in London, White said, "I got a lot of jobs already," and added, "I'm sure we'll have something to talk about after that." He did not say whether he is interested. CNN cited a source familiar as saying White had declined the idea. White also posted an Instagram photo of himself at the White House briefing room lectern, writing "On to the next chapter", though the BBC said it was unclear if that was tongue-in-cheek. White House communications director Steven Cheung encouraged him on X.

The job has been vacant since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days in. Trump's post came after Republicans lost their congressional majorities in the midterms. Trump called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked him to bring several UFC fighters along.

White already leads UFC and Power Slap, has launched Zuffa Boxing, and sits on Meta's board. He is a longtime Trump ally who spoke at Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024. What comes out of Monday's meeting is the next thing to watch.

A drone attack on a military base in Santa Rosa del Sur, in northern Colombia, killed three soldiers and wounded at least 16, the armed forces said Saturday. Authorities have not said who was responsible. Social media footage showed smoke rising after three explosions and soldiers sheltering behind sandbags, according to Al Jazeera.

President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on X that those behind the attack "will have nowhere to hide" and that every attack on soldiers strengthens the government's resolve. The area, in the foothills of the San Lucas mountains, is rich in gold mines and has long been disputed by armed groups including the Gulf Clan, the ELN and smaller groups led by former FARC members.

Al Jazeera reported that violence has intensified in several rural areas since de la Espriella, a conservative, took office in August. He cancelled peace talks with rebel groups and has used more air strikes, deployed more troops in some cities and created joint task forces to protect strategic assets such as a pipeline. His government argues that armed groups used ceasefires under the previous government to tighten their grip on rural areas. Some groups have responded by stepping up attacks on the armed forces.

Last week, missiles made from gas canisters hit a base in Tolima province, killing four civilians, including a two-month-old baby. Police in Cucuta have been attacked several times with remotely activated bombs. ACLED counted 34 bomb or explosive attacks by state forces and illegal armed groups in the four weeks to October 16, 9 percent above last year's four-week average.

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck western Shizuoka Prefecture in central Japan at 1:04am local time on Sunday, injuring more than 20 people, according to local media and authorities cited by Al Jazeera. The Japan Meteorological Agency said the quake was about 40 kilometers (25 miles) deep. Kyodo news agency said the injured were in Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures, and the Associated Press reported that some fell on stairs while trying to flee.

Japanese television showed shattered shop windows and glass on streets, and a bookstore with piles of fallen books. A wide area was affected, including Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Nara, Yamanashi Prefecture, where Mount Fuji is located, and Gifu. Kyodo reported that no tsunami warning was issued, and the quake was not felt in Tokyo.

The meteorological agency warned people to be ready for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially over the next two to three days. Official Ayataka Ebita asked people to watch for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects of rainfall. He said no apparent change had been detected so far in the Nankai Trough, an undersea trench where scientists say a megaquake could occur.

Some local train services were suspended, and Shinkansen bullet trains ran at slower speeds in affected areas as a precaution. JR Central said Tokaido Shinkansen trains between Shizuoka and Gifu-Hashima stations were delayed after safety checks. Aftershocks and the weather are the main things to watch in the coming days.

Activists say two more Uyghur men held in Thailand could be deported to China, and one of them has said he would be "like a slave" if sent back, according to The Guardian. Human rights groups say the men were recently moved to an immigration detention center. They fear Thai authorities may again give in to pressure from Beijing.

Last year Thailand forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite appeals from the men and the UN. The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, and the UN says the returnees' whereabouts remain unknown. The two men were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghurs detained in 2014 near the Malaysian border after fleeing China. They had served a seven-year sentence for offenses tied to a January 2020 escape attempt from immigration detention.

Elaine Pearson of Human Rights Watch called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. Thailand's national security council chief, Chaipruak Doungprapat, told reporters the men and three other Uyghurs still in prison have outstanding arrest warrants in China. Marzeyya Kasem, the girlfriend of one of the men, questioned why China did not seek an Interpol red notice in 2014, noting that he was a minor when he left China.

China's foreign ministry spokesperson said cooperation with Thailand against cross-border crime is consistent with both countries' laws and international practice. Beijing has defended its Xinjiang policies as aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism. Thailand's foreign ministry declined to comment. It is not clear whether China has made a formal extradition request.

Authorities on El Hierro, one of Spain's Canary Islands, have declared an emergency and asked the government in Madrid for help after a surge of migrants and refugees arriving by boat. Alpidio Armas, head of the island's governing council, told Spanish television on Saturday that the sharp increase in arrivals was very worrying and that the declaration aims to create a framework for cooperation with higher-level institutions.

Local authorities say more than 3,300 people have reached the island, home to about 11,400 residents, on about 30 boats since the start of November. Officials are seeking temporary accommodation, and Armas said conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable". Regional leader Fernando Clavijo, quoted by Reuters, called the situation "absolutely unsustainable". He said buses have been diverted to migration work and medical staff brought from other islands, and that the pace is approaching 2024 record levels and on some days exceeds it.

The Atlantic route from West Africa is one of the world's deadliest. AFP reported that two people were found dead on a boat heading for the Canaries this week, and five others are believed to have died during the voyage. At least nine migrants have died off the islands in recent weeks.

Arrivals peaked at more than 46,000 in 2024, then fell sharply with tighter surveillance and cooperation with origin and transit countries. Spain's Interior Ministry counted 13,327 sea arrivals from January to October, 5.5 percent fewer than a year earlier. Patrols have pushed departures further south, making crossings longer. Whether Madrid will respond to the request was not stated in the source text.

Republicans are debating whether to keep to Trumpism or change course after losing the House and the Senate in the 2026 midterms, according to the BBC. The party also lost governorships and state legislatures in places such as Texas and Kansas, where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades.

Reactions vary. The BBC reports that outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis called the results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans." Vice-President JD Vance blamed public anger over the war with Iran, said the party could turn things around, and predicted "a lot of infighting and arguing." Steve Bannon predicted a "civil war," blamed the economy and foreign wars, and urged Trump to double down on mass deportations. Strategist Whit Ayres said a significant part of the party is non-Maga, and "that's a majority now."

Three days after the election, Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. The BBC says this signals Trump does not plan to moderate. Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, told NPR it shows the administration is "not rolling over." Roberts said he supports the Iran war but that Trump should declare victory, because its economic effects hurt Republicans. He said Heritage still backs reciprocal tariffs, though in a more limited form. Democrats' responses to these moves were not included in the supplied pages.

The BBC cites a New York Times analysis finding Latino support for Democratic candidates rose 29 percentage points from 2024 to 2026, and support among voters aged 18 to 29 rose 33 points. Pre-election polling showed widespread disapproval of Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and Iran. The BBC says it is too early to tell which Republican faction will prevail.

NASA announced a set of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand its Moon Base effort, covering commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure. The agency made the announcement at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It says the goal is a sustained presence at the Moon's South Pole.

For cargo delivery, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of Commercial Lunar Payload Services, called CLPS 2. The framework is a 10-year, multiple-award contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA also raised the value of the current CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion. The original contract stays in place through November 2028, with deliveries to be completed through November 2033.

NASA is also moving ahead with PROMISE, the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration. The six-wheeled rover will be powered by nuclear energy so it can operate through long lunar nights and in permanently shadowed regions thought to hold ice. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will build it from spare flight components and engineering test models for the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers. It will carry a drill able to reach about 3 feet below the surface, spectrometers, sensors and cameras. NASA is targeting a late 2028 launch and an 18-month mission.

Blue Origin received a $94 million base contract, with an option worth another $140 million based on performance, to deliver PROMISE using its Mark 1 lander. NASA also awarded six task orders under its VADR launch services contract to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space to transport Moon Base cargo.

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood told CNBC on Friday that investor worry about markets reinforces her optimism. U.S. stocks sold off sharply on Thursday, reversing an initial rally after the midterm elections. AI-related stocks led the decline and pushed the Nasdaq Composite into correction territory. Tech shares made a tentative recovery on Friday.

According to CNBC, much of Thursday's selling reflected concern that a Democrat-led Congress could slow data center construction. Worries about AI spending, cash flow, debt and circular financing have also caused several bouts of volatility this year. Wood described a "wall of worry" over markets. She said she remembers the tech and telecom bubble, when there was little concern, and that today's worry suggests "a more durable bull market."

Wood said one thing that could become a "showstopper" is the rising cost of capital. CNBC reports that interest rates and bond yields have climbed sharply this year as the U.S.-Iran war pushes up inflation, and corporate bond yields have risen too. Wood said the correction is partly caused by bond markets. She argued that AI has high fixed costs, which brings bond investors into technology in a way they were not before. She added that companies expecting debt to speed their growth are barely affected by interest rates.

Her advice was to identify high-conviction positions: take some profits in rallies and buy back in during sell-offs. She said Ark has concentrated on those names, and that its SpaceX position has risen. Wood called the turbulence "two steps forward, one step back" and said she expects the equity rally to continue in 2027.

Democrats' wins in this week's midterms could have a large effect on the tech industry, according to TechCrunch. Voters in dozens of local ballot measures rejected data centers, and they elected politicians, such as Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on restricting them. TechCrunch's Equity podcast hosts discussed the results.

Sean O'Kane noted that Elon Musk, one of the biggest data center builders and the largest donor to the Republican Party, "seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars." His companies are headquartered in a state that has turned about as blue as it could. The article adds a correction: many ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those passed.

The hosts differed on how much data centers drove the results. Anthony Ha said anti-AI and anti-data center sentiment seemed to be a big part of the Democratic gains, though not on the ballot everywhere. He said the issue is bipartisan in many ways but that Democrats seemed better at harnessing it, and he expects the next two years to be harder for tech companies. Kirsten Korosec said data centers probably did not bring voters to the polls, but have become a grassroots issue partly because of secretive approval processes, including NDAs for officials, in water-scarce areas.

Korosec said OpenAI has already released a "compute campus policy blueprint" that drops NDAs and promises less secrecy. Ha said the new name is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, which have become a toxic phrase, and wondered whether it will take.

Artificial intelligence is speeding up parts of hiring, and that could push recruitment agencies to rethink how they charge, CNBC reports. Agencies often take a percentage of a placed candidate's first-year salary. David Berwick of Adria Solutions said that if an agency is simply finding CVs and forwarding them, AI makes that service "increasingly difficult to justify."

CNBC cites a 2026 Bullhorn survey of nearly 300 recruitment professionals in the U.K. and Ireland. It found 37% said AI had made candidate screening between 26% and 50% faster. LinkedIn's 2025 UK report found recruiters using generative AI saved an average of 18% of their working week. Adecco said its U.K. AI agents save about 15% of time spent on recruitment processes, and that humans still make hiring decisions.

Views on fees differ. Matt Collingwood of VIQU Group said he sees every reason for fees to hold or rise if the value delivered grows, and reported his firm's turnover is up 47% over 18 months. Even so, he predicted only a third of today's agencies may survive the next five years. James Wright of Velocity Leadership said AI lets him do work that once needed a team of five, and he expects 60 to 70% of staff at the large executive search firms to lose their jobs.

Paddy Lambros of AI platform Dex argued fees are high because hiring is inefficient, and that having candidates and clients each use AI is a waste. Chris Stirling of Stirling Q&R said value will lie in judging candidates, adding that "the fee now has to be earned on the hard part."

Demand for Labubu, the collectible monsters sold in sealed "blind boxes," appears to be cooling, according to the BBC. Pop Mart, the Beijing-based maker, recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September fell by as much as 50% from a year earlier. Revenue in the United States dropped by at least 70%. Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.

The BBC says the craze once made Pop Mart worth more than Hasbro and Mattel combined. Labubu launched in 2019, was worn by celebrities and drew long queues. Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and is worth nearly $24bn, but its shares are down more than 50% from last year's peak. Analyst Samer El Hajjar says investors worry the success was a viral moment rather than lasting loyalty. Ashley Dudarenok of ChoZan says the sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart raised production.

Collectors describe the shift. Content creator Ensito, who left his tech job in 2024 and has spent over $50,000 on more than 400 Labubus, says his videos struggle to reach 10,000 views and he has turned to other trends. Rivals such as Sonny Angels, Smiski and Miniso's blind boxes have gained ground.
Pop Mart has invested in a Beijing theme park and announced a Labubu film. Dudarenok says the real test next year is whether it can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it.

Three studies presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's scientific sessions in Chicago examined lowering blood pressure in people who have had a stroke or have type 2 diabetes, according to STAT. The results were mixed. One small trial tested a common diuretic after stroke, one tested a lower blood pressure goal after stroke, and one tested a lower goal in diabetes.

The first trial, REDUCE, was led by Jordana Cohen of the University of Pennsylvania. Patients given the cheap diuretic spironolactone right after a stroke were more likely than those on usual care to have blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg three months later. The trial measured blood pressure, not cardiovascular outcomes, and was presented as an abstract that has not been published in a journal.

OPTIMAL-STROKE, a larger Brazilian trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine, compared a systolic target of 120 mm Hg or lower with the recommended 140. Participants who aimed for the lower number were significantly less likely to die or have cardiovascular events within four years. Researchers said reaching it requires medical supervision, including kidney monitoring. There was no increase in end-stage renal disease, dialysis or deaths, though some kidney markers were off.

OPTIMAL-DIABETES, also in the journal, found neutral results. Aiming below 120 rather than 140 did not reduce major cardiovascular events or deaths in patients with type 2 diabetes. Shawna Nesbitt of UT Southwestern said treatment might be approached in a more nuanced way. Bruce Ovbiagele of UCSF noted that U.S. post-stroke care is fragmented across specialists, raising the question of who manages the medications.

Nintendo released a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Thursday, after years of rumors. The BBC's Tom Gerken reviews it, noting the 1998 original remains the highest-rated game on Metacritic. Nintendo chose not to reinvent the game, producing something that plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

Gerken, who grew up with the original, says it feels familiar. Producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told him modern players expect more to be shown on screen rather than imagined. The updated graphics are more cartoonish, and series producer Eiji Aonuma said testers found the Skulltula House too scary at first, so it was adjusted to keep the original's balance.

Several YouTubers gave positive verdicts. Mike Channell of Outside Xbox said the remake was made meticulously, with controls that match modern expectations. Ed King, known as Zeltik, praised its detail and charm, and StrawHatMidas called it a perfect way to bring the classic back.

There are changes, notably to the Water Temple. Aonuma said he most wanted to alter it because of its reputation for being very difficult. Players can now switch heavy boots more easily and use camera orientation. Gerken calls the free camera a significant improvement.

His main criticism is that familiarity sometimes made tasks and puzzles too easy, and he wonders if Nintendo played it too safe and wishes there had been more changes. Fujibayashi said the team kept the essence the original developers intended.
